extracted.intended_audience: Indian legal scholars, patent practitioners, policymakers, and microbiologists interested in patenting microorganisms in India
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and procedural criteria, statutory interpretation, international obligations, and practical requirements for obtaining patents on microorganisms and microbiological processes under Indian law and related treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbes which undergone with genetical or any artificial modification. Not being found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes 'substantial human intervention' as a threshold: original/natural forms are discoveries and not patentable; only microbes modified by human action (e.g., genetic modification) can qualify. This criterion was singled out by the Mashelkar Expert Committee as central to examining applications involving microorganisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbe or microbiological processes must be new and not previously found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty must be demonstrated for the microbe or the process; genome sequences can be deposited in DNA databanks (NCBI, DDBJ, EMBL) to document novelty. Native/natural forms are considered discoveries (Sec 3(d)) and thus not novel for patentability purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness (inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbe must not be an obvious variation of a previously known microbe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must assess whether the claimed microorganism or process involves an inventive step beyond routine or obvious modifications of known organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbe or microbiological processes must have a specific function and used for manufacturing particular products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must show a specific, practical application (e.g., production of antibiotics, enzymes, vaccines, biofuels). The Mashelkar committee and TRIPS-consistent standards require demonstrable industrial application.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPS categories of patentable microbiological inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the patentable micro-biological inventions according to the TRIPS agreement are: (i) process of producing a new microorganism; (ii) new microorganism as produced by the defined process; (iii) new microorganism per se; and (iv) process of cultivation or otherwise using a known or new microorganism to form multiplied microorganism itself (e.g., vaccine or edible biomass) or by-products (e.g., antibiotic, enzyme, toxin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS Article 27 requires members to allow patents for microorganisms and microbiological processes (subject to enumerated exceptions). The article lists these TRIPS-consistent categories as guidance for what kinds of microbial inventions are patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) discovery exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of known efficacy, or mere discovery of any new property/new use for a known substance, is excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to microorganisms, Sec 3(d) can bar patenting mere discoveries of natural forms or minor variants unless there is enhanced efficacy or a new product/resulting process. The article cites Sec 3(d) to explain why native forms are treated as discoveries and not inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(j) and statutory treatment of microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patents (Amendment) Act 2002 inserted the term 'microorganism' in Sec 3(j); India allows patenting for microorganisms but lacks a clear statutory definition leading to confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Sec 3(j)'s insertion and subsequent ambiguity: while amendments permit microorganisms and microbiological processes, policy and manual/guidelines are needed to clarify scope (e.g., whether viruses are covered). The Mashelkar committee recommended strict guidelines for examination focusing on substantial human intervention and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty: deposit recognition and IDA requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Budapest Treaty an applicant who deposits microorganisms with any 'international depositary authority' (IDA) need not deposit in every country; a deposit at one recognized IDA is recognized in all contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 7 and Article 6(2) set facility requirements for becoming an IDA. India is a party and hosts IDAs (NCCS, IMTECH; NAIMCC slated). Applicants must deposit biological material with a recognized IDA to satisfy patent procedure deposit requirements across treaty countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample deposition durations and patent deposit handling
rubrics_metrics.description: WDCM sample deposition durations: General Deposit – 5 Years; Safe Deposit – 5 Years; Patent Deposit – 30 Years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patent purposes, deposits are maintained confidentially for up to 30 years. The article also notes practical storage requirements (e.g., lyophilized form) to preserve microorganism viability for long-term patent deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and storage requirements for microbial patent submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Microorganisms are determined via phenotypical characterization, 16S rRNA analysis, MALDI-TOF analysis, etc., and should be stored (e.g., lyophilized) for preservation before patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends specific laboratory characterizations (phenotype, 16S rRNA, MALDI-TOF) to support claims and to emphasize secure storage and deposit prior to patent examination; these practical evidentiary elements aid examination and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application content and examination criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must provide detailed information about the microorganism's characteristics, isolation methods, and potential industrial applications; the patent office examines novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The procedure involves filing with full disclosure, possible additional government guidelines for biotechnological inventions, consideration of ethical/environmental implications, and rigorous examination by patent examiners who must be satisfied before grant. The Mashelkar committee urged stricter examination guidelines for microbial claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimum patent term is about 20 years from the date of registration; the patent is charged per annum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard patent term/time-to-expiry and periodic maintenance/renewal fees apply; the article notes the typical 20-year term for granted patents on microorganisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microbial strain patent vs microbial genome sequence patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbial strain patent covers the physical microorganism (culture, derivatives, parts); microbial genome sequence patent covers the genetic information (DNA sequence, gene expression data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strain patents protect the organism and its uses; genome-sequence patents protect specific genetic information for defined uses. The article highlights different legal and commercial implications and typical bases for grant (unique properties vs novel genetic sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of viruses (current ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viruses are discussed as special class: viruses are considered 'non-living' in some senses and Section 3(j) 'does not cover non living microorganism (virus)'; there is uncertainty about patentability of viruses under Indian law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The COVID-19 pandemic raised questions about virus patentability; the article recommends that viruses be defined separately in the patent manual and that examination guidelines for virus-related applications be issued promptly to remove uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key judicial precedents affecting microorganism patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable cases: Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980, US) held artificially constructed microorganism patentable; Dimminaco A.G. v. Controller of Patents & Designs (Kolkata HC, 2001) held manufacture/process yielding products containing living organisms can be patentable; Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013) relevant to pharmaceutical/product patents and Sec 3(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precedents frame how courts and patent offices may treat microorganisms and processes: artificial construction/substantial human intervention and the patentability of processes that yield living products are supported in precedent. Novartis illustrates Sec 3(d)'s application in pharma contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mashelkar Expert Committee recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Expert Committee (Dr. R.A. Mashelkar, 2006) suggested microorganisms can be patentable and recommended strict guidelines for examination focusing on 'substantial human intervention and utility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee's report is cited as recommending formulation of clear examination guidelines to reduce confusion arising from lack of statutory definitions; its emphasis reinforces the human intervention and utility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms and system weaknesses to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms include inconsistent standards for patentability, weak/poorly enforced patents, lack of safeguards for traditional knowledge and biodiversity, lack of openness/uniformity in examination, backlog of applications, inadequate funding and examiner capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These critiques point to systemic evaluation criteria for the patent regime itself: proposals in the article include increased funding, more examiners, clearer guidelines/manuals, and safeguards for traditional knowledge and biodiversity to ensure fairness and quality in microbial patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological Diversity Act definition implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(c) of the Biological Diversity Act 2002 defines 'biological resources' to include 'plants, animals and micro-organisms or parts thereof, their genetic material and by-products (excluding value added products) with actual or potential use or value', but excludes human genetic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition connects biodiversity regulation to patent regime considerations (e.g., access and benefit-sharing, prior informed consent), and impacts how microbial resources are treated in patent disclosures and compliance.
